utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, during cross-examination, Mr. Milosevic spoke with you about Dusan Jovic, TO commander in Glina appointed by you, and the exhibit was actually tab 118 of Exhibit 352. Did Mr. Jovic actually fulfill his position and did he command the TO units in Glina during any military operations in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. -- Dr. Dusan Jovic was appointed at the end of July 1991, but he was not able to take up his positions, perform his duties, because of the obstructions that were going on, first of all, in the structures in Dvor, Kostajnica, Petrinja, or rather, the North Banija division. He performed the function as president of the municipal Assembly of Glina. That was the authority and competence he had.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who obstructed him taking up the position of TO commander; which organisations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the structures, the commander of the Central Banija, Bojan Bajagic, and then the JNA units and police units in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You also appointed, on the 4th of October, 1991, Major Cupovic and other reserve officers to be -- to form the TO staff in Glina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that's tab 134, Your Honours, from the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they actually fulfill and take up the position or were they also obstructed? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness come closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly how it happened, what the events were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you come a little bit closer to the microphone so that the interpreters can hear you better. Mr. Milosevic also spoke with you about Dr. Radovan Markovic, and he referred to a letter to Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this document was not tendered so far, Your Honours, and therefore I would like to put it to the witness and also tender it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look at the Serbian version of this document. It is a letter from Dr. Markovic to Arkan in Belgrade of the 25th of November, 1991, in relation to the participation of Arkan's unit in the defence of Petrinja, and it says here: "We agree with the proposition that members of the Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan's unit, participate in fightings on the JNA and TO positions in the municipality of Petrinja. The unit will be commanded by a senior officer, and the unit will be part of and under the command of the commander of the 2nd Motorised Battalion of the 622nd Motorised Brigade." And I would like to know from you who made this proposition that Arkan's unit participate in the fighting on the JNA and TO positions. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as I can see from here, it is Dr. Radovan Markovic, president of the Municipal Assembly of Petrinja who gave his permission for that and agreed to it, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And there is also mentioned the 622nd Motorised Brigade. Is that a JNA brigade or a TO unit? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a JNA brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know who commanded this brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but Slobodan Tarbuk was there. Whether he was the commander of the brigade or the whole garrison in Petrinja, I'm not quite sure. Colonel Slobodan Tarbuk, whether he was commander of the brigade or the garrison, I'm not quite sure, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is a Bogdan Ercegovac mentioned in this letter. Do you know whether he was a JNA officer or what his position was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a JNA officer, I know that. As far as I know, he was appointed commander of the TO in Petrinja for one particular detachment in Petrinja, or rather probably. It was renamed the motorised battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The interpreters still have difficulties to understand you. Please speak into the microphones. Did Arkan actually take part in the fighting in Petrinja in November 1991, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to this 622nd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we are moving from the document, we should give it an exhibit number first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 352, tab 172.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the 622nd Motorised Brigade, I would like to put to the witness another exhibit which is also not yet tendered. It is an order of the Commander Spiro Nikolic of the 1st Operational Group Command, dated 19 October, 1991, and it's placing TO units under JNA units. And we have here the mentioned in this order the 622nd Motorised Brigade. Witness, looking at the document at the head, the header and the format and the signature, is that an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at least according to what I can see here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Major General Spiro Nikolic, was he the commander of the 1st Operational Group Command, and where was this group command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the command at Samarica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, during cross-examination, put to you that you forced Colonel Trbojevic to effect mobilisation in Gracac and Donji Lapac and to expel all Croats from Gracac. You have already addressed the mobilisation of volunteers for the 1st Light Brigade, and we would not have to comment on this any more. But my question is were Croats expelled from Gracac, and if so, did you order this, or who?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Gracac region, the Croats were expelled, yes, during the combat and fighting with the 1st Partizan Brigade and previously through the operations led by Frenki Simatovic, and Mile Martic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last phrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last phrase. The interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operations led by Milan Martic, and before the 1st Partizan Brigade went into operation to deblock the warehouses in Svetilok [phoen], and in the Gracac area, the Croatian village of Lovinac they did go into operation. Frenki, or Franjo Simatovic as he was known in Gracac, and Milan Martic with mortars -- with a mortar unit. They were the first to open fire on the village of Lovinac, and thus expel the Croats from the Gracac area, municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were Croatian villages including Lovinac set on fire? That's what you discussed with Mr. Milosevic. Were they set on fire and who did it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The villages were set on fire. They were looted, and this was done by those structures, the structures that attacked them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And which structures did attack them? Is that what you just mentioned, Frenki?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to Kijevo, Mr. Milosevic questioned to you and put to you that there was no coordination between General Mladic and the Martic police. And I would like to put to you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The document which is also not yet an exhibit. And it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want the last one exhibited or not, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 352, tab 173.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the next exhibit that I would like to be exhibited is the 16th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina held in Banja Luka on the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It is an --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's an enormous bundle of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, and I only want to discuss with the witness page 46 of the English, of the translation, and page 35 of the Serbian version. It's just about Kijevo and what Mr. Mladic himself on this session said about Kijevo. It's 37, page 37 [sic], and there's just one quote.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Witness, for you, it's marked. And it is Mr. Mladic speaking, General Mladic speaking, about what happened in Kijevo, and he says the following: "The Knin Corps was successful because under a single command in the zone of the Corps were the JNA, the Territorial Defence forces, and Martic's police. Isn't that right, Martic? And because he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it marked in the English at page 46?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Page 47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thought you said 46.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, page 47.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. And I continue: "And because he and I, I call him and say, give me 40 policemen here at Kijevo, and you took part in the fighting, isn't that right, Milan? And we did what we had planned, and we planned -- and we will have artillery here, and this artillery acts."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, from the whole document, you can see that also Mr. Milan Martic is present during the Assembly meeting in Banja Luka. And so General Mladic refers to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, were you aware that such an Assembly meeting took place in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did this quote from General Mladic, did it actually reflect what happened in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Both in your -- I want to move now to another chapter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 352, tab 174.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, both in your examination-in-chief and while questioned by Mr. Milosevic you spoke about the appointment of the TO main staff in October and November 1991 and the arrival of the officers Maksic, Kasum, and Vuletic in Knin. And Mr. Milosevic put to you that those officers actually volunteered to serve in the TO. And I would like to know from you when they came, when they came to Knin, did they continue to be members of the JNA, or did they quit their service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were on the payroll of the JNA, or rather, they were in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did they transfer back to the JNA or VJ at a later point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went back to the army of Yugoslavia. They were transferred there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher in this relation, I would like to put to the witness another document. And it is an order. It's an order by Gojko Krstic, the chief of the personnel administration of the VJ headquarters of the 22nd April, 1992, addressed to the TO of the RSK on the deployment of 72 officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Witness, when you look at the position, there is -- there are 72 people listed in this document. And on position 1, you see Kasum Dusan, and on position 5 you see Aleksandar Vuletic. Are these the people that arrived, and are they still on the JNA members, or rather VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are the two people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And looking at the document at the format, including the header and the person who signs it, is this an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Major General Gojko Krstic, in which administration was he chief? Do you know which administration of the VJ it is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personnel administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to have this exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 352, tab 175.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to this matter, I also would like to have to the witness the Exhibit -- a new exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This previous document, I'd like to indicate in it that it is not signed by Gojko Krstic. The signature here is by somebody who says that he is a sergeant first class who is signing, and not the signature of Major General Gojko Krstic. I don't see Gojko Krstic's signature there, so I don't know whether the witness says he recognises the signature of the sergeant first class. He can't recognise the signature of General Gojko Krstic because he hasn't signed his name there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll take note of that, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness didn't say he identifies the... The next document is a list of military staff of the VJ temporarily deployed in the RSK TO submitted by General Torbica, commander of the RSK headquarters, to Colonel Medakovic of the VJ personnel administration of the 19th October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And looking at the document, can you comment on its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is authentic. Milan Torbica was indeed the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If you look at the first person listed, it is Milan Torbica; and on the first page, the 15th person listed is Dusan Kasum; and on page 3, under the units in Kordun we have the first person listed as Cedomir Bulat, whom you had mentioned previously as a JNA commander; and listed under Lika on page 7 is Milan Suput, the person that you also mentioned previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can that be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 352, tab 176.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to Colonel Djujic, my question would be, was he also, despite his position in the TO, was he paid by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Djujic, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to General Mrksic, Mr. Milosevic questioned you about his origin. And my question to you is despite the fact that General Mrksic had family roots in the RSK, before he was appointed RSK army commander, was he in the VJ, and did he continue to be a VJ officer? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the Kertes intercept, the intercept Braco-Radovan Karadzic, it's tab 28 of Exhibit 352, Mr. Milosevic put to you that the Vojvodina was the bread basket of the former Yugoslavia, and that you cannot conclude that they were speaking about anything else than food and deliveries of medicine. My question is: Was Mihajlo Kertes, whom you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. described as the member of the MUP, Serbia, involved in eight deliveries of humanitarian character? Do you know whether he ever dealt with such deliveries?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you received humanitarian aid, who would usually organise that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would come in through different channels, through individuals --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Institutions, not channels. Interpreters' correction.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would the MUP Serbia be involved in it, in these kind of deliveries?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Given the date of the intercept, that's June 1991, did you in the Krajina receive medicine, food, and blankets from Vojvodina? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we move from there, for the record, it should be noted it's not Exhibit 352. The Registry point out it's Exhibit 353, tab 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I'm sorry, then, I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to other -- Mr. Tapuskovic actually put to you that in relation to intercepts in July and August 1991 when Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Milosevic spoke about steps to be taken and plans, he said that at that time, Slovenia and Croatia were already independent and therefore why should they speak about plans. My question to you is at that time, was there a moratorium agreed upon so that Slovenia and Croatia postpone their declaration of independence until October?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It was the Brioni agreement with the representatives of the European Community, and the moratorium held true for three months.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the Mirkovci oil wells, you said to a question of Mr. Milosevic that oil was produced in Mirkovci and then processed in Pancevo. Pancevo, is that in Serbia near Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the Pancevo refinery? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who was the manager. It was a state-owned or socially owned company, oil refinery.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that quotas of the processed oil for RSK and RS existed. Who decided about the quotas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mikelic, Stanisic, or rather, the DB and Mikelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that is the dispute they had you referred to during your testimony about the quotas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic put to you in relation to the army, the involvement of the JNA in Croatia, he put to you that in relation to the involvement of the JNA in Croatia, the JNA intervened only for two matters, that is, to separate the clashing parties, and to deblock their own barracks. Is this a proper description of their conduct in the Serb-controlled regions, in the SAOs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA intervened in the first place in order to deploy in the SAO regions, and then beyond them, and to keep that territory in the state that was being created by Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was the JNA in summer 1991 a neutral force that protected both the Serbs and the Croats equally, or did it side with one side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the Serb side; that is, on the side of Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see my half hour is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you asking for a little longer?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You aren't. Good. Thank you very much. Mr. Babic, that does conclude your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are two technical matters left open. Two exhibits that Mr. Milosevic wanted to tender were marked for identification, and it's, first of all, the list, the list with the 5.000 names. And the problem that the Prosecution has with this list, it is actually the following: You cannot see from the list who produced it, when, and on which basis, what is the foundation of this list. And I think it should be only marked for identification until this foundation is laid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to the book, I have to say that also the Prosecution would like to tender in the course of this trial a few books without the author being present. And I would say if Mr. Milosevic would accept that, too, we are willing to accept this book as well. But it would be -- we wouldn't do it without any discussion on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have doubts about books because of what they contain and the difficulties of saying what status they should have. It may be convenient if we mark it for identification, and at a suitable time, when you have the books that you have in mind, we can perhaps look at them all together, apply the same principles to them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That's convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Our next witness has protection, and accordingly, may we go into closed session briefly. And when we have gone into closed session, there's a couple of short administration matters that I'd like to raise as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I explain, now that we're in open session, that this witness is Witness C-025, who has already taken the solemn declaration. And although I think the witness has yet to look at this particular map, may I invite him please to be shown on the overhead projector page 23 of our atlas, Exhibit 336. And it's the right-hand page, and it's the top left-hand half of the right-hand page, please. That's perfect. Thank you very much. Little bit to the left. A bit further to the left. Perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness C-025, you're looking at a map with which you may not be familiar, having prepared to give evidence with a different map. But look at this map, please. Does this map show the area of Baranja? Do we see it to be bordered at the north by the boundary with Hungary; to the east by the boundary with Serbia marked substantially by the Danube River; and to the south through Osijek by the Drava River?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At the material time with which we are concerned, when the boundary with Hungary was closed, were there two bridges passing into Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serbia on the east, one at Batina in the north, and the other one at Erdut immediately east of Osijek to the south of this area of Baranja?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not in Baranja. Erdut is not in the area of Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there at one stage a bridge at Osijek? Did it become destroyed? If so, when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify the question. Across which river? Because Osijek had a bridge across the Drava River.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, across that river.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a bridge. It was destroyed by the Croatian police or army sometime in the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Paragraph 3: Before the conflict, C-025, was the multi-ethnic SDP popular in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the SDS party grow in influence over time, and did that match in any way the growth of the HDZ on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could the usher just leave the map on the overhead projector. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was this area visited by any radical Serbian politicians; and if so, can you name them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the radical politicians, there was Vojislav Seselj who came, and Mr. Paroski would also come.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What, if any, influence or effect did their visits have on interethnic relations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very purpose of their visit was national awakening among the Serbian people in Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did that have any effect on the non-Serbs in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that very point in time, that is, during the visits themselves, not so much. But later on, during the conflict, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: By the first half of August 1991, what measure of control did Serbs have over the area of Baranja?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of Baranja was in the hands of the Serbs. A village in the immediate vicinity of Osijek, Bilje, was still not under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there a meeting of the Serb Territorial Defence in Jagodnjak, which we can see south of Beli Manastir and north-west of Osijek?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you learn of what happened at that meeting; and if so, what was the rank or position, but do not name the person, the rank or position of the person who informed you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about that meeting from the commander of the local staff of which I, too, was a member. The meeting was held in Jagodnjak. Representatives of all TO staffs from Baranja and representatives of the SDS attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was the discussion at the meeting? What influence, if any, did the political party the SDS have at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was linked to the organisation of the attack on the village of Bilje. So it was of an operative military nature, whereas representatives of the SDS, that is, two representatives of the top leadership of that party, attended the meeting purely to get information and to familiarise themselves with the operation and to assist in the organisation as sufficient men needed to be recruited to participate in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. We'll find Bilje on the map just a little north of Osijek. At the time of this meeting, could you estimate what percentage of local Territorial Defence commanders were members of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Percentage-wise, perhaps around 80 per cent of the staff commanders were in the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I want to turn to another topic, Crisis Staffs. But before I do so, in summary, please, the ethnic composition of Baranja before the conflict and the ethnic composition by estimation by mid-1991, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Baranja is a multi-ethnic region with three ethnicities represented, the Croatian, Serbian, and Hungarian having roughly an equal share. After the outbreak of the conflict, this ratio was changed in favour of the Serbs, which means that the non-Serbs left Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you be in a position to estimate the percentage of the population that was Serb by that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the non-Serbs left Baranja, so the Serbs from the Osijek area came in to Baranja so that the percentage of Serbs -- there were 30 per cent to begin with. But the percentage increased more and more afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Crisis Staffs, the Chamber may be familiar with this, but in case they are not, a word from you about them. Did Crisis Staffs have a peacetime and proper function? If so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staffs were set up in peacetime, and their task was to give assistance to the population and citizens in case of elemental disasters such as floods, droughts, et cetera. So to assist the population in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: By the time of and in the conflict, did the SDS have any say or influence over the appointment of presidents of local Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I may come back to that. But let's move on to this: As non-Serbs were leaving the area, did decisions have to be made about their real estate and other property? If so, who dealt with it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The property that was left behind was placed at the disposal, or rather taken over by the Crisis Staffs, and the procedure for this was as follows: The immovables were sealed and the property was listed, recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How was it allocated, and were there incoming Serbs from other parts of Croatia who had to be accommodated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That same property, the property that had been sealed and listed, was given to other Serbs from Croatia who came in to the area. Both individually and in organised fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did this influx of Serbs from elsewhere and the allocation of property to them result in any consequences or anxieties for the non-Serbs remaining in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The greater influx of Serbs from Croatia took place towards the end of 1991. Western Slavonia, that is, from Western Slavonia, the Serbs were coming in to Baranja. And as I said, they were accommodated in the houses that had been left empty and facilities. There were villages in which these Serbs, Serb refugees, became the majority, the majority population. And that is where the problems arose with the long-standing locals, non-Serbs, who had remained in those places. Usually they were elderly persons whose children had left and gone to Croatia and they had stayed on to look after the property.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Insofar as those people suffered any problems, whether of harassment or worse, did the local Serb authorities take any steps to protect them or to control such harassment or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first few months, no, they did not. The first few months in which these sort of clashes occurred, violence was tolerated.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Turning now to the Territorial Defence and very briefly, as the ethnic composition changed, was there a change in the chain of command or the effective chain of command of the Territorial Defence for Baranja?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it originally responsive to authorities in Zagreb? Did that position change?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did it indeed cease to become responsive to Zagreb; and if so, to whom was it responsive thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence of Baranja, on its territory, received a superior command, and that was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there any pattern of replacement of local Territorial Defence commanders on political grounds?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the pattern was that the most suitable individual would be looked for to implement the policy. It wasn't essential whether they had any previous military knowledge or education; it was purely based on political rating.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And political acceptability being judged by what approach to the problem? What was required of these military commanders by the political leadership?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking about the local commanders, the commanders of the local TO staffs, which meant that the basic prerequisite was for the person to be a Serb or rather a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the course of the conflict generally, was war activity in Baranja itself very limited, and if so can you tell the learned Judges at which sites there was real fighting, site or sites?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was real fighting on two occasions in the Baranja region. First, the first battle was fought over the place called Bilje, which is where the Serbs attacked in order to take control of the village of Bilje. And this took place at the end of August 1991. At the beginning of 1992, however, the Croatian army launched a breakthrough operation on the Baranja territory along the axis and in the direction of the village of Torjanci, which was the second battle that took place in Baranja, along with a few other incidents and attempted attacks on border huts along the border north-west of Baranja, in the area -- or rather, towards the Hungarian border and the Drava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, Torjanci is just visible on the overhead projector because it's on the fold of the page, and it's immediately to the left of Petrovo Selo, top, left-hand corner of the area we're concerned with. As always, it's in the fold of the map. Places always are.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Apart from those incidents of fighting, Witness C-025, was there any sporadic or regular looting of property in this area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was looting of property, yes. At the beginning, it was more intense and it lessened afterwards as the situation calmed down and as the property was listed. The looting lost its strength.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What part, if any, did local Territorial Defence commanders play in the looting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were individual cases where the commanders were involved because they had at their disposal the means of transport which, under those circumstances, was vital. I'm talking about trucks and similar vehicles. So that when the first front lines were taken, in the villages where they were accommodated, in the houses and property that had been left behind when the people had left, they would take it away, take that property away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can I deal now with the degree to which local Serbs in the Baranja area were armed. Was there a pattern of local Serbs obtaining weapons? If so, when and from whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. Arming systematically started when the Plitvice Lakes events took place, and the occurrences in Borovo Selo, which means sometime in May 1991 onwards. And illegally, through illegal transports, weapons were brought into the village of Jagodnjak, and then further distribution of weapons was conducted through the members of the SDS, and it was distributed in the other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber can find Jagodnjak north-west of Osijek and effectively due south of Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you yourself, Witness C-025, obtain a weapon? If so, from what category of person? Don't be specific as to any location.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received it from a member of the SDS. I was invited to go to his home and fetch the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you went there, did you see any other weapons? If so, what types of weapons did you see?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see weapons. Usually infantry-type weapons with a few hand-held Zolja-type rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From where did you understand those weapons to have come?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from those rocket launchers, all the other weapons were out of date, outdated weapons. That is to say, weapons that had been manufactured at some previous date from some military stockpiles. They weren't up-to-date state-of-the-art infantry weapons; they were old-fashioned mostly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If not from Baranja itself, from which region or state had this collection of weapons come, to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It came from Yugoslavia, or rather, from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'll return to paragraph 14, if and when we next go into private session. Paragraph 15: By the end of July 1991, was there any JNA presence in the Baranja area? If so, where?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. The JNA was present in two locations. It was permanently stationed -- there was a unit permanently stationed in Beli Manastir, and another unit on the bridge between Baranja and Serbia, or rather, in the village of Batina; on the bridge itself and up above the village as a protection to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The unit based in Beli Manastir, what sort of unit was that and where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a unit which provided security along the state border towards the Republic of Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know where the -- what sort of unit was it? Was it a mechanised brigade or something different?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an infantry unit, but when the conflict broke out, it was reinforced with some armoured personnel carriers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And from where had they come? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had come in from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: By "Yugoslavia," do you mean Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean Serbia, that's right. At that time, to all intents and purposes, the country was still Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At the end of September 1991, was the local Serb Territorial Defence commander a man Borivoje Dobrokes, or Dobrokes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just yes or no, did you discover or see him to be assisted by officers from outside Baranja? If so, how many, give us their rank and origins.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There were officers from the Yugoslav army, or rather the JNA as it was at the time. And they dealt with organisational problems for the TO staff and headquarters in Baranja itself. They were high-ranking officers, and their rank was colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From which town had they come? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that one of them was from Belgrade and that he was a lecturer at one of the high military schools in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Following the Vance Plan and the withdrawal of the JNA from Baranja, were any JNA or Serbian-origin officers left in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they serve in any sense or way with the local Serb Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they have any other connection with Baranja itself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps a small portion of it did, either family ties or others. But most of them did not have any connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We've now dealt with various component parts of the way of life as affected by the conflict. Could you in a few sentences, for the learned Judges, help us with what life was like. You've told us about the two areas of real conflict. Was life normal? Did businesses go on? Did farming get done throughout the period of the conflict, or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for life at that time in Baranja, we couldn't say that life was normal because of the circumstances themselves. War was looming, and it was autumn. Baranja is an agricultural area, a farming area. So it was a time of crop collection. And the conflict escalated at that time so that this made things rather difficult and the crops were taken in late. And it was not done properly. And this was later reflected on the situation in the whole region. Supplies were only possible through the bridge in Batina. That was the only physical link with Serbia and the other territories, and that is where goods came and went from mostly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Water and electricity, what was their availability?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for electricity, the lines went towards Croatia. A compromise was struck between the TO staff in Baranja and the Croatian side so that electrical power could come in. And they promised not to attack the economic facilities or touch the economic facilities, those that were in the reach of the JNA or Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And finally, a couple of homey as it were examples, with the change of ethnic composition, would people still be able to meet on a multi-ethnic basis in public places like bars, or would there be any change in behaviour? And socially, did people change their behaviour so far as dealing with other ethnicities is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether we can say generally speaking that this took place, well, we could, but that depended on the environment itself. And as we said that Baranja was a multi-ethnic area, in the areas in which the Serbs had become the vast majority, situations of that type did arise from time to time. But in the other areas where the population remained mixed, this was not as evident. There was not so much evidence of polarisation on an ethnic basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we go into private session for paragraphs 14 and 18 to 20.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the second half of 1991, was there a pattern of non-Serbs in Baranja being arrested? If so, in what circumstances and for what reasons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conflict, arrests were very frequent. There were no special criteria or rules in that respect. People -- non-Serbs were mostly arrested for various reasons, among others, their wealth or their affiliation with the HDZ, or because of certain unsettled accounts from the past of a legal nature or purely personal nature. Anyone who carried weapons would arrest others. And then towards the end of September and the beginning of October, as time went on, these arrests were reduced. Actually, a state -- the rule of law was established in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Until the return to that rule of law, where were these people detained? How were they treated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arrested people were taken to a Detention Centre in the SUP building in Beli Manastir where more or less all of them were mistreated physically and mentally. And then from that Detention Centre, they were sent to Dalj or Borovo Selo to be exchanged for captured persons on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That exchange, where it occurred, would have involved passage over one or other of the bridges at Batina or Erdut. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question isn't quite clear to me. Exchange? There were never exchanges on any of those bridges.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Very well. My error. You've spoken of the exchange of these people. In the course of the exchange, would they have had to pass over one or other of those bridges in transports?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the transport from Beli Manastir to Dalj or Borovo Selo, at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Batina, at the Batina bridge, they had to leave Baranja, and then to enter the eastern parts of the territory of the Republic of Srpska Krajina and on to Dalj and Borovo Selo. They had to cross the bridge twice at Erdut the second time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At each of those bridges, were there representatives of Yugoslavia or Serbia who would have been in a position to see the transports and to discover what was on the transports?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that both bridges were protected on the Krajina side, by the Krajina police, and on the Yugoslav side, by the Yugoslav police, which also controlled the crossing of each persons. So I think that they were able to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Approximately how many people, to your knowledge, were arrested and transferred or intended to be transferred in that way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, which is not too precise, about 50 to 80 people were arrested and transported for the purpose of exchange during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Of those people, 50 to 80, were there any who were subsequently not accounted for and not seen again?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite a large number of the people intended to be exchanged were never exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you obtain information later as to what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later we learned that those people were executed. Or rather, some were thrown into the Danube River; some were buried in mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And finally on this topic, what was the particular vehicle or type of vehicle in which they were transported?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vehicle was adjusted -- it was really used for the transport of forestry workers, like a lorry, which instead of a tarpaulin had a kind of container like a minibus, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we go into private session for the last time to deal with matters between paragraphs 23 and 28.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we have a map, please, which is much like the map we have at the moment but this is one that the witness can mark. And it will be... Thank you very much. Exhibit 326, tab 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we need to exhibit it first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's the correct tab, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If you can take a pen, please, on this map because we can't mark -- a bit further up, please. That's fine, thank you very much. You've referred to a place called Tikves. Is that also something connected to somewhere called Tito's castle?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The residence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you just mark on this map roughly where it is. And also I think there's a national park of which this is a part.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that's the area of Tikves, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In that area, what did you see of an anti-terrorism unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That unit was in Baranja on two occasions, twice; when the conflict broke out and sometime in 1995 as well. It was always located in -- within the compound of this residence of Tito's.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On the first occasion -- and you haven't given the year, but on the first occasion, what was it doing, apparently?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this unit turned up, or rather, the first contacts with the unit, were in the building itself, the MUP building in Beli Manastir. That was the first time that I saw the members of that particular unit, and they were wearing the red berets and different types of uniform, different to the ones we would see in our area most commonly. Some of them slept in the MUP building in Beli Manastir itself because there are dormitories in the building. And some of them would spend the night there and they would come into our office for a cup of coffee or tea or whatever. And when we talked to them, we learned why they were there, why they had arrived. In the Beli Manastir town itself at that time, certain groups of individuals terrorised the populace, if I can put it that way. There were problems that arose with respect to the division of the property that had been left behind; facilities, coffeeshops, pastry shops, et cetera. And this Red Beret group intervened several times over the next few days, and it shamed the local heavy men. They felt threatened with the arrival, with the advent of this unit, and how they were going about their business in Beli Manastir itself. It put to shame these thugs and bandits, local ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where had this group of men wearing red berets apparently come from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had come from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When in Tito's residence or castle, how secure or sealed was that location?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the specific features of the property itself, it lies in a physical area of forest, several hundred hectares. There are entrance gates or ramps which it is easy to control. And these units did control the area and permitted entry or banned entry into the property.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Two other details about these troops: With what weapons were they equipped and what method of interpersonal communication did they have? What sort of radios and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had automatic rifles. That was standard. However, what was specific was that the rifle wasn't worn on a belt across the shoulder, but it was carried in the person's hand. And they also had communication devices, Motorolas, et cetera, to be able to communicate amongst themselves, which was rather -- which only the TO and JNA -- which was very rather in TO and JNA units at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The second appearance of this group or men similarly attired was in 1995. What did they do then? Where did you first encounter them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that particular year, they tried to sort of reeducate the people, if I can put it that way. They engaged in terror, intimidating the population. Because the Serbs had also left Baranja. Now, to prevent this from going on in the future, that unit sowed terror amongst the population, and they wanted the people to calm down, to stay put, and to train the young men who were of military age and who had not undergone military training. So there were training centres for soldiers. And there was another activity that the unit engaged in, and that was to legalise different vehicles, passenger vehicles, heavy duty vehicles. That means to do all the paperwork because those vehicles had arrived into the area through unlawful means. And so they did all the paperwork to make them -- to legalise them. And then they left the territory. Individuals -- there was a racketeering going on where extortions were made from the rich well-to-do Serbs in the area. They were blackmailed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there a Colonel Vasilje Mijovic, who was involved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Exactly what did he do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the direct commander of the unit. The unit's immediate commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the unit have anything to do with local criminals?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Well, in particular?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In particular, they tried to have the better-trained criminals work under them. So there were professionals for different things, like, for example, for stolen vehicles. This man Zeljko, nicknamed Gavro, was in change of them. Then there was Predrag Radetic, nicknamed Brada or "beard." There were weapons, professionals.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You've touched on this already, but just to complete this part of your testimony, was there a transfer of property, as well as a seizing of property, was there a transfer of property out of the Baranja area; and if so, what part did these Red Berets have to play in that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was transfer of property both private and what was known as socially owned property. At one point in time, the Red Berets were the ones who controlled this going and coming of property and persons at the Batina bridge. And they had their own checkpoints that they set up on the communication lines along the roads running into Batina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There was in fact one other question that I ought to have got by way of detail. Did Colonel Mijovic establish two training centres? If so, where were they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did set up a training centre for young soldiers in the Baranja Petrovo Selo area and in the Knezevi Vinogradi.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm sorry. The first can be seen towards the top left of the map on the overhead projector at the moment, and Knezevi can also be seen pretty well above and to the left of the blue mark. One exhibit for this witness to deal with. May we have a look at it, please. Your Honour, it's a document that I hope to produce formally through another witness, and therefore I invite this witness's comment upon it. If the usher could be good enough to show the -- display the original, first of all, on the overhead projector, that is, the original in Cyrillic so that we can see what it is. The report page, which is about three pages from -- four pages from the back, just look at that, see what it is or what it appears to be. It's headed "Explanation" and it's called "Abuse of positions by members of the anti-terrorist operations." And if you now, please, Mr. Usher, detach the original and hand that to the witness and place the English version on the overhead projector. And I'll just read it, or some of it, and ask for comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness C-025, this document in English reads, and you can follow it in the original: "The attached documentation shows some of the abuses on the part of the commander of the ATD, Colonel Mijovic, and other officers in smuggling, resale and taking of cars from Baranja." Next paragraph: "Through our sources, we have obtained access to a part of the documentation indicating and proving the illegal registration of vehicles most frequently stolen in European countries and brought to Baranja where their papers were legalised in something as an authorised service. There is no information in the safes about previous owners." And then next paragraph: "Based on talks with a source, Mijovic has so far taken away 25 to 27 vehicles." Next paragraph but one: "Besides this through his man, a member of his unit whom they called Brada, or 'beard', Mijovic twice seriously threatened the head of the car registration service not to stick his nose into the papers too much. The man went to Mijovic's for treatment and is very frightened." And then it goes on to make further allegations in general. You needn't look at it in detail, you've seen the document in preparation. Does the matter recorded here fit with, or not, your own experience of what this unit was doing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be exhibited. It's promised to be established in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mark it for identification. Get the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 357, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have the document. May I be given a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry it didn't find its way to the accused already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of your package of documents you got. But have another one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, only if it was handed over this morning, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Finally, paragraph 34, were you aware, Witness C-025, of killings in the region by men dressed in the uniform of milicija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were those killings investigated? Did anything ever happen to the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The perpetrators were never punished. I can't say 100 per cent that nobody was held accountable. The police did go to conduct on-the-crime-site investigations, and all the operations necessary in proceedings running up to bringing charges against the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to trouble with paragraph 35, although should anybody want to ask the witness about it, I would ask that it be done in closed session, for obvious reasons. In case there was an error or similar as a result of the way I asked a question, can I just go back to paragraph 8 on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Remember, Witness C-025, we were talking about Crisis Staffs at an earlier stage, and I asked you about the appointment of the presidents of Crisis Staffs. Thinking back to that period of time, to your recollection, did the SDS party regularly or from time to time take any part in appointing the leadership of the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it was: When the conflicts broke out, the commanders of the Crisis Staffs were in those posts, according to the statutes of the local communities. When the conflict escalated or with the passage of time, and as the situation in Baranja changed, so did proportionately the influence wielded by the SDS party itself in all segments, and among others, this applied to the nomination and appointment of members to the Crisis Staffs, and they themselves would elect their president, or rather, their commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness C-025.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Witness, why did you say previously that SDS had no influence over Crisis Staff? You remember the question asked by Mr. Nice, and you said no. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because I consider that we have two periods; the period prior to the breakout of the conflict and the period after the conflict had broken out, because the Crisis Staffs existed in peacetime before the war, as they did afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the marked map, the Prosecutor's Exhibit 326, tab 12, the marked map will be tab 12.C-025.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. C-025, is it true that you were given instructions as to the way you should testify here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I received in writing a piece of paper as to the way one testifies. It's in the witness room, how one should behave here. I don't understand your question. What kind of instructions are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify my question. Apart from receiving instructions regarding behaviour in the courtroom, you're telling us that you did not receive any other instructions about the way you should testify here. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And is it true that you had previous contact with representatives of POA, or the counter-intelligence agency from Zagreb? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the man you contacted -- his name is Snajder.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anyone by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know Snajder from the counter-intelligence agency of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know his assistant, Vatroslav Vrdoljak?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't meet with him either?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any conversations in which an operative of the centre of this counter-intelligence agency of theirs, that is, the security service of Osijek, Milenko Pekic and Josip N - so he's from your area - you never had any contact with him? You never saw him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know Pekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who do you know? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Pekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Only Pekic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know Josip.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was this conversation over your preparations for testifying in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? What do you mean? Where was this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was a conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm asking you where. Can you be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you assume there is information about that and tapes of those conversations? You probably don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then please answer the following questions with precision. Is it true that on Wednesday, the 23rd of October, 2002, you received a telephone call by -- from Milenko Pekic who made an appointment with you for the next day at 7.45, that you should meet near the centre for the counter-intelligence agency in Osijek because you needed to go to Zagreb for a meeting with the bosses of this agency to discuss your coming to The Hague? Is it true that he phoned -- that Pekic Milenko phoned you on the 23rd of October, made an appointment with you for the next day, and from there, you were to go to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As in those days, the plan was for you to go to The Hague at the beginning of November. Is it true that he told you that you had to report to the OTP on the 6th of November, 2002, and that you would be staying there until the 11th of November, 2002?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, fine. Very well. Who asked Pekic to do this and who asked some influence to be brought to bear on you, we'll come to that later. Is it true that on Thursday, on the 24th of October at the appointed time, in front of the centre of the security service, now called the counter-intelligence agency, you met with Pekic and a certain Josip, on the 24th of October, 2002? Please be very precise and try and refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meet Mr. Pekic very frequently because we go fishing together. As for Mr. Josip, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you meet this Pekic that you meet often on the 24th of October in front of the centre where he works in Osijek?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You meet often, but you're sure that you didn't meet on that particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I don't go to that building. We meet because we both have boats tied close to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And did you go to Zagreb in an official vehicle, a Golf IV vehicle, with Zagreb license plates, and that during the trip, you were told that in Zagreb you would be talking to the bosses and that these would be good people and that you were free to ask them anything you want and that you should not be cautious about anything, that you can talk to them freely? Do you remember that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that upon arriving in Zagreb, you went to the brewery called Medvedgrad not far from the Vatroslav Lisinski concert hall, where two persons were waiting for you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went to Sesvete, to a motel to spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you went to Sesvete to a motel there. What its name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Antunovic. There's a petrol station and a motel right next to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were two people waiting for you there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, why did you go to that motel in Sesvete?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To spend the night there for the trip to come here because I had an early flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that this person who travelled with you introduced you to his boss and said that his name was Snajder, and then to his assistant who introduced himself by the name of Vrdoljak?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't meet with them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that after a brief introduction, Snajder addressed you and thanked you for agreeing to testify and for your overall efforts and said that he was aware of your work and the assistance you were giving the service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about any such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that you are here under oath to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know those people you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that on that occasion, this boss told you that he was aware of the problems you had at work, but that you should forget those problems because they wouldn't be repeated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say no once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't talk to anyone about this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people that you are mentioning, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well who did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion in that motel and on your way to Zagreb and when you spoke about the preparations for coming here.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't talk to anyone linked to preparations and to coming here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that later on, Snajder said that he had read your whole statement given to the investigators and that he would suggest that should there be a chance that you should emphasise that the preparations for the aggression started as early as 1989 by the JNA against the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was a suggestion made to you to speak about certain operations, Proboj 1, 2, 3, et cetera? Did you talk about these things with anyone at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was one linked to Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of those operations that you are mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And did anyone suggest to you that you should say that it was quite clear some time ago that the crisis could not be resolved by peaceful means and that the JNA started arming and contacting Serb extremists and party leaders long ago? Was that suggestion made to you or not? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about. No one made any suggestions of any kind to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did they tell you that as a witness, you will not be talking about specific cases but that you should highlight the chain of command, that is, give examples how Mijovic's unit was under some sort of administration in Belgrade and received orders from it? Were you told to say that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one talked to me in connection with my preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who drove you to the Zagreb airport?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went in my own car. In my own car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You drove there yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it's parked at the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And Pekic didn't go with you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this on the 6th of November?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date now. But anyway, I drove in my van, my own car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they didn't leave you their telephone numbers or e-mail address or anything for contact?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have Mr. Pekic's telephone number. But that is on a private basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So privately, you do mix, you do socialise. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what is his position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly his position. I know the work he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of work does he do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's working in the former state security; that is, SZU.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in the current state security as well, but it's no longer called that. It's called the counter-intelligence agency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. SZU with the new name that it now has.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were you told then that Pekic had been given instructions to provide counter-intelligence protection for you, and he also gave instructions to give misinformation should your identity be disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that that misinformation should be made public through the media and through radio Glas Slavonije. Did he tell you anything along those lines?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then how, or rather let me correct myself. In what way do they take part in providing protective measures? You're a protected witness, and you're living over there. So how does the service we're referring to participate in providing protective measures for you?
