Is it just through Pekic or do you have contacts with any other people in connection with those protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours I'm very concerned about this line of cross-examination bearing in mind the witness is corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, doesn't seem to be of any relevance anyway. So move on to another topic, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I think that with regard to credibility of this witness, it is indeed relevant whether he had first been instructed by the Croatian intelligence service regarding his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's denied that. Now what you can't ask, because it may compromise his own security, is details of that security. It's not relevant. What you can ask is what connection, if any, he has with that state security service. You can ask him that if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did they tell you when you left the country your passport would not be stamped so there wouldn't be any traces, and if they do stamp your passport here that you would have to have it exchanged when you got back?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And there is a stamp in my passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But let me ask you quite precisely: Is it true that most of the information you have given in your testimony is actually information of the Croatian service, especially the information regarding some criminal offences of which you had mostly heard about, as you said in the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The information comes from my own life, my own memory, and from my operational work during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you were not able directly to collect such information through your direct work in the area.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are all persons from my surroundings, most of whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you're claiming in your statement on page 2, last paragraph, that the SDS influenced the activities of the TO in Baranja. Were you a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then how can you assert that when you were not a member or a member of the SDS leadership? How do you know to what extent they were influential over certain institutions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew people who were in the SDS that I collaborated with closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you heard this from people in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was there any other party in Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period - in 1991 - no, later yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1990, there was the League of Communists of Croatia as far as I know, and later it was renamed the SDP. And most of the population voted for the League of Communists of Croatia in 1990. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And later, was the socialist party formed in Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were attempts for parties to develop, but the SDS took a decision that all this should be stopped until better times, that the SDS should remain as the only party. And then later on others could be formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now go on --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question at 11.12.06.08 transgresses the rule about closed session. We've got to be very careful in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why this mystery, Mr. May, because this witness is not saying anything that he himself saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So very well. The SDS had the greatest influence. And evidence on that is on your second page, the meeting of local staff of the TO at Jagodnjak at which two from the SDS leadership from present. When there was a discussion about the Bilje operation. Is it true that you were not present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were not present at that meeting, how do you know what was discussed and who was present?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the commander of my staff was there. And I learned about it from him, talking to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the commander of your staff briefed you about everything that happened at that meeting where they were discussing some sort of an operation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the most important points, that one of my task and that of him and some other people was to try and find 40 men to take part in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And on the basis of what did you come to the conclusion that apart from the presence of those two SDS officials, that they were giving instructions to the TO commanders what they should do, or were they among themselves agreeing on what should be done to strengthen the defence of Baranja?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about the operative part of the meeting, nor was that of any interest to me. That is actually what they agreed on at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know what competencies were determined at that meeting; you're just saying that two SDS officials were present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know what their role was, nor whether they gave instructions for that operation or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Tell me, please, in connection with this allegation that you made again on page 2, last paragraph, regarding the conflict between the TO and the Croatian paramilitary grouping in Bilje, in August 1991, is it true that Bilje was a stronghold of the MUP and the National Guards Corps, the Zengas, ZNGs, in those days?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This concentration of the guards, the Croatian guards, and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. MUPs, was it a threat to the population in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure you could say that outside the village of Bilje since there was a kind of separation line already around the village of Bilje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what they were doing, they did on their side of that separation line?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they didn't breakthrough your line of separation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there wasn't a single case of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been sporadic exchanges of fire, but no breakthrough or any serious operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does exchange of fire mean? Did they open fire at you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was shooting from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct to be more specific about this event that it was there a conflict occurred between local Serbs and Croats in Bilje?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In August 1991, was there an attack by the Croatian National Guards Corps and the MUP on the Serbs in Bilje or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were attacks, but several Serbs entered the village of Bilje. And as they recognised one another, their identities were disclosed, and then fire was opened. And two or three Serbs were killed in Bilje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, two Serbs were killed in Bilje.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they entered from other villages to enter Bilje, and they knew that the separation line was there and that the Zengas and the MUP were in Bilje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So they knew they were there, and because these two Serbs entered the village, they were killed there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they entered armed. One was even wearing a MUP uniform, that is, the uniform of the Croatian police, and he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And those two, did they go there to attack Bilje?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what their intention was. They went there on their own initiative. They didn't report to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did the two of them go to Bilje? Surely those two didn't go to attack Bilje when there was such a concentration of MUP and Zengas in Bilje. They didn't expect, I suppose, anyone to shoot at them.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly because they were wearing this uniform they didn't expect to be recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They wore uniforms just as the others were wearing uniforms, they were working in the police, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they came to Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No you said they came to Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: They were staying in a territory over which the Serbs had control, and then they entered a territory under Croatian control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were they by profession?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was an inspector in the Croatian MUP, and the other one, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was a policeman?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I know about this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know about this one. And let's leave the other one aside, that you're not sure about. But this one you know about was an inspector in the Croatian MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he was wearing the uniform of the Croatian MUP so he didn't put on anybody else's uniform. He wore the uniform of the institution he was employed in.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he was killed because he was a Serb. Isn't that right? Or because he attacked Bilje all on his own?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before he attacked Bilje himself, he had left the Croatian MUP. He had crossed over into the other territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then he attacked Bilje alone? I see. And did you hear that on the 17th of August, 1991, Milos Zivanovic was killed in Bilje?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many Serbs were living in Bilje?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe some 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many would that be, 20 per cent Serbs in Bilje?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Bilje has about 4 to 4 and a half thousand inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. If that is the population, 20 per cent would be shall we say 4.800. Is that right? Did the Zengas and MUPs terrorise the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most Serbs had left. Some did stay behind. But I can't be more precise in telling you exactly the number of Serbs that stayed and the number that fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did they flee Bilje?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why did the Croats flee from Baranja? Nobody was hurting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I know that no one was hurting the Croats in Baranja. But just a moment ago, I'm glad you have confirmed that. A moment ago you said that where the environment was more or less purely Serb, there was more demonstration against, and more chaotic, and where there was a mixed population, the situation was -- the relationships were more tolerant. So in mixed environments, people were not aggressive towards each other, and they led a normal life.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time has come for a break. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have an hour and ten minutes, if you want it, Mr. Milosevic, with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, in the information which I received for this witness, it said that the opposite side plans to have -- to conduct its examination-in-chief for six hours. Now quite suddenly, that examination-in-chief was radically reduced so that I have many more questions than would be possible for me to put in the hour and ten minutes you've just allotted me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, well, you make a start, and if necessary, we'll review the position at the end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall continue according to the notes I have made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke about the Crisis Staffs. Is it true that the existence of the Crisis Staffs was pursuant to the laws prevalent in Yugoslavia at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it also true that the Crisis Staffs commanders were members of the local government authorities, that is to say, as a rule, the presidents of the executive councils of those municipalities would be members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking before the conflict took place or after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about how it was pursuant to the law and how the de facto state was.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The presidents of the local communities as a rule were Crisis Staff commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did they continue to do later on, the presidents of the local communities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the beginning of August or rather the end of September, the military and civilian functions were separated. Crisis Staffs for civil matters were set up and Crisis Staffs for military matters were set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 17th of August, 1991, a meeting was held of the Crisis Staff in Beli Manastir at which were present in addition to the members of the Crisis Staff all the former presidents of the Municipal Assembly of Beli Manastir and the former deputies and most of them were Croats, deputies of the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you happen to know that the kommandir, the MUP commander, head, or chief, whatever you'd like to call him, in Beli Manastir was Prdogut Ante, a Croat, and after the Crisis Staff meeting was held on that same day, the 17th of August, in Beli Manastir, said quite literally the following, I understood the contents of the meeting differently, I expected you to give me permission to raze Jagodnjak to the ground, and Jagodnjak is a fairly large Serbian village otherwise with many Serb inhabitants. And he asked that he be allowed to raze it to the ground, and he said he would be able to complete this within a space of 24 hours, that he had the strength and power to do that. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the command of the Crisis Staff in Beli Manastir was Lazar Brnovic, who did not take up that position following the chain of the Serbian Democratic Party but was nominated by the official Croatian organs and he otherwise was of Montenegrin by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before the war, the TO municipality Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. The TO municipality Crisis Staff, you say. Very well. Now, in view of the fact that you yourself dealt with the organisation of the TO during the examination-in-chief, you also mentioned the relationship with the JNA and with the JNA. Do you know that the Yugoslav state presidency, following a proposal of the federal Secretariat for National Defence, already in 1986 passed a decision to reform the command of the army into the command of the military districts under whose command was the TO in the district, on that territory?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that that was done because during the mass movement Croatia attempted to arm --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... no point in going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I agree. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that the republican staffs of Territorial Defence were subordinate to the federal Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the republican staffs of the Territorial Defence were not, by the same token, under the competencies of the presidents of the Republics or the governments of Republics, but they came under the federal government and its institution the Secretariat for National Defence, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also right that the municipal Territorial Defence was responsible to the Territorial Defence in Zagreb right up to the creation of SAO Krajina, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that republican staff was subordinated to the federal National Defence Secretariat. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it also true that the weapons from the Beli Manastir Territorial Defence staff was transferred to the barracks in Beli Manastir for security purposes exclusively?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the Garrison, you mentioned the garrison, and you were asked about the presence of the JNA and where the JNA had come from, come to be there. Is it clear that the JNA didn't come from anywhere because the JNA was on the territory as a regular army throughout a period of 50 years?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my presentation that there was a stationed unit of the JNA in Beli Manastir, and that a portion that was not linked to Baranja was in -- at the Batina bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the Beli Manastir garrison was a border garrison that catered to the border huts along the Yugoslav state borders between Yugoslavia and Hungary. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this was entrusted to the army to protect and defend because there was a danger of the uncontrolled use of weapons on the part of the local inhabitants. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that at the beginning of 1990, there were attempts to turn the TO of Croatia into a Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the media, what I was able to learn that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know or did you hear about the fact that General Spegelj, in his book "The Recollection of Soldiers" noted himself that in Croatia what came to be understood was that the TO of Croatia was in fact Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not read the book, but I saw the tape linked to Mr. Spegelj, the footage of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you remember that the idea to turn the TO of Croatia into a Croatian army was not an original concept of those present-day people, but at the beginning of the 1970s, the leaders of the mass ^ epoch, the mass movement, endeavoured to form the youth units and the republican organs would have all the power and authority over them. I assume you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know something about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in those 1970s, the public prosecutor of the Republic of Croatia proposed that any chauvinistic outbreaks --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I, while I'm on my feet, make this point: The accused seems to think that because there was an estimate of six hours at some stage, presumably based on the length of the witness statement, that gives him some right to six hours. The entitlement of an accused person is to cross-examine on the basis of the evidence in chief prima facie. We would resist any suggestion that he's simply entitled to a figure that was an original estimate. His cross-examination must be responsive, broadly speaking, to the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter for the Trial Chamber. This is an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. accused in person. He must be entitled to some latitude facing, as he is, extremely serious charges. On the other hand, there is most certainly a limit, as he knows, on the time which he will have available. It most certainly won't be six hours. Try and finish in the time that we've suggested, Mr. Milosevic. I'll consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we can sit until 2.00, and we'll give you until then to deploy your cross-examination. So you should aim to make your main points fairly early on to ensure that they are covered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, it is very difficult for me now at this juncture to restructure my questions while I'm conducting the cross-examination itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You do not -- don't be misled by any of the time estimates which the Prosecution give. Sometimes they are out on the grounds that they are far too short, and other times they are too long. But move on. It would be helpful, rather than general questions, some of which can be proved by evidence and some of which are matters which we've heard about before, if you concentrated on the specific questions which you can ask this witness which he's likely to know about of his own knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the main staff of the Territorial Defence of Baranja had handed out weapons to the local TO units pursuant to the laws that were in force at the time? And you have this on page 3, last paragraph of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the fact that individuals frequently looted and that property was taken.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the police take any steps to prevent this, to stop this, and was it indeed halted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gradually, yes. At the very beginning of the conflict, it was impossible to prevent this from happening. However, as time went by and until the end of 1991, this was reduced to some legal frameworks and perpetrators were prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when the atmosphere was one of chaos at the very beginning of the conflict, it wasn't possible for them to stop this, but then later measures bore fruit and that unlawful acts were stopped. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you personally see anybody taking off somebody else's property anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you see, for example? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on several occasions, I saw furniture being taken away, appliances, household appliances, and even tractors, sewing machines, livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did the people take all this off to; home?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they took it to their own homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was the local population that did that, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the population, the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it true that in Baranja after the elections held in 1990, a referendum was organised at which most of the population voted for the option that if Baranja proclaimed itself to be independent, that it should remain within Yugoslavia nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that none of you at the time spoke about any kind of Greater Serbia; people wanted to live in Yugoslavia, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we stated our views through the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was a multi-ethnic environment, and most of the population of different ethnic groups reacted in that way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the majority won the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So not only the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, not only the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to skip over a few questions which I don't feel are indispensable, in view of the curtailed time that I have, although they are all important questions, you said on page 3 of your statement, paragraph 4, that after those first elections, the Serbs became afraid that Croatia would proclaim its independence. Why were the Serbs afraid of that independence on the part of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It was a kind of popular opinion, opinion held by the majority of Serbs. And I'm sure this has its historical roots.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, I think it would be highly beneficial if Your Honours did have a copy of the statement given to the investigators for the Prosecution because Mr. Slobodan Milosevic has referred back to the statement several times. It is dated the 10th of March, 2001. That was the date of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said that there was some sort of fear. Tell me, did the expulsion of the Serbs from the constitution of Croatia as a constituent peoples in 1990 and the abolishment of the Cyrillic script, and schools for Serb children, the discriminatory laws, and the series of events that followed, were those reasons why the Serbs feared living in an independent Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes. But in view of the referendum, it wasn't only the Serbs that took part in the referendum, I think that others shared that opinion, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what we're talking about, it was precisely in that multi-ethnic environment that we had great support for Yugoslavia, not only the part of the Serbs but on the part of the Hungarians, Croats, and other ethnicities living in the area. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that in only four months, June, July, August, and September of 1990 in Croatia, over 10.000 Serbs were dismissed from their jobs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know when the decision was made to set up the Croatian National Guard Corps, and how this formation of the Croatian National Guard Corps affected the general mood that prevailed amongst the population, not only Serbs but all the inhabitants living in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the details about its establishment, but I refer back to the referendum. I assume it was formed on the basis of some sort of groundwork.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that the decision taken by the Croatian leadership to import weapons from abroad illegally and to withdraw what was in the hands of the police force with Serb police members, did this affect the deterioration of the political situation in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yes. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true, do you happen to remember a decision taken by the Yugoslav State Presidency at the beginning of January 1991 to disarm the paramilitary units, among which the Croatian National Guard Corps was the first, so-called Zengas, that was never put into practice and the Zengas were never disarmed. But do you remember that decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well I don't recall the decision but I do know that kind of topic, this issue, was written about by the information media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the HDZ policy became more radical as time went by, and that the elements found their inspiration in the former independent state of Croatia had come to the fore?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about Tudjman's statement that there would only be 5 per cent Serbs in Croatia in the final analysis?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was bandied about by the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was the fear that the population felt in Baranja precisely for all these reasons the proclamation of independence, et cetera, was it the reason for which the SAO Slavonia, Western Srem and Baranja was proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly, but the decision was to remain within the frameworks of Yugoslavia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the proclamation of the region? Did it mean that these regions de facto had separated and seceded from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that those regions had their own organs, institutions, government, police force, army, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And those regions were de facto and de jure regions outside Serbia. I don't suppose that's in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that in the Territorial Defence for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, were only local inhabitants who actually lived in the area, they were members of that body?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some volunteers too, from Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Volunteers you say who had family ties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, family ties or ties of friendship, ties of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're just saying what I said a moment ago. You say it on page 3, paragraph 2, of your statement, and in the last paragraph as well of page 4, paragraphs 1, 2, and 3 of your statement you say precisely that, that there were only locals living in the area.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of them, the vast majority were. All military able men from the ages of 18 to 60 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the law in force at the time all able-bodied men between 18 and 60 years of age responded to the mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 25th of August, 1991, there was a session of pro-Yugoslav parties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question at 13.02.53 transgresses the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Milosevic, don't ask questions like that except in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This does not reveal the identity of the witness, Mr. May. There's so many people here from the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may reveal where he comes from. Anything that's liable to do that, you should be aware of.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 25th of August, there was a meeting of pro-Yugoslav parties? This was their coordinating committee, with several members of the staff of the TO of Baranja. Are you aware of that meeting held on the 25th of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of a meeting at which a decision was taken on the appointment of the executive council of Beli Manastir, the secretary of the SUP, and various other appointments were confirmed for the commanders of the TO in Baranja and agreement reached on the distribution of positions, those responsible for civilian affairs, the TO towards the border with Croatia, all these things were discussed at the meeting that was held on that date? You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that meeting, but I do remember when these appointments were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 30th of August, there were talks between representatives of the authorities, the SUP and the TO of Beli Manastir and Valpovo, Valpovo which is in Croatia? And their main options, the options of the meeting, were to create conditions of life free of conflict, free of violence, the aim being to ensure conditions for the peaceful life of all the inhabitants of the region. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about that meeting, but I assume in my earlier testimony I did refer to something linked to electricity supply. And that was linked to that meeting, I think. Should electricity be cut, a countermeasure could be action against economic enterprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 30th of August, over Beli Manastir radio, it was announced that all citizens who had sought refuge, and the majority were Croats, could return to their homes and that they are free to harvest their fields and gardens, that they can sow wheat normally, and a special call was made to those from the Belje agricultural combine because there was a lot of work to do on the fields. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I didn't hear that report, though the situation was such as to warrant such measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on that same day, that is, the 30th of August, when over Beli Manastir radio, there was this call for the refugees, Croatian refugees to return, that members of the Zengas opened fire on the Serbian villages of Jagodnjak and Poljeman [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were frequent exchanges of fire. I can't tell you the exact dates, but there were frequent exchanges of mortar fire in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on that same day, a sabotage group of the Zengas with 60-millimetre mortars and rifle grenades, and it was headed by Stevo Kitak [phoen], a policeman, attacked the Jelen estate, that is, the Djitica [phoen] plant, which is also known as Pustara?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several such sabotage actions, planting of trip mines, and anti-armour mines, and they came too close to our positions because the line itself was quite unusual, there was a no man's land covered with thick woods and brush.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that members of the Zengas on the 2nd of September kidnapped Savo Sekanic, a Serb, a peasant from Jagodnjak, and that the International Red Cross was informed about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know or had you heard that on the 3rd of September, 1991, from the Croatian leadership through Glavas, an order was issued for the collective emigration of the Croats from Bilje but that only the men of military age should stay behind. Do you remember that order of theirs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we agree that in Baranja in general, there was very little military activity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your examination-in-chief KOG. What is KOG, K-O-G?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counterintelligence group engaged in counterintelligence in the field, and it may also cover civilians, because according to the law of National Defence, all men of -- able-bodied men of military age are subject to that law on defence and can be covered by KOG. The military service was divided into operatives outside the barracks which were in plainclothes and people in uniform in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'm wrong, maybe I misheard you, please correct me if I did. You mentioned that KOG armed the Serb population. Did you say that or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The associates of KOG would receive truckloads of weapons. When I say associates, those associates became associates after they were armed. I knew who were the men who obtained weapons, but I didn't know what they represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you get weapons from that group that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were you ever present when KOG armed anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present. Physically I was not present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that the counterintelligence group supervised the reserve JNA force. What kind of supervision do you mean? You mention this on page 41 but last paragraph in the sense of counterintelligence protection, they were able to apply all methods, informative interviews, technical methods and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you mean that the service was collecting intelligence information which is its normal work, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, you mentioned that somebody called Dragisa Radic, Stojan Sekanic, and Damir Zuzic, Rajko Mrdja, all from the area. One is from Darda, the other from Knezevo, the other from Batina, from Beli Manastir, that they were collaborators of the KOG. Did you personally see them engaged in any specific activities as part of that collaboration? What is the grounds for you to say that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through subsequent work in the field, we would meet. Operatives of the state security and operatives of KOG on the same assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that in June 1991, I will not mention the name of the local inhabitant because this could reveal your identity or be considered to reveal your identity, you received an M48 rifle, a rifle that was no longer in use in the JNA. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he an SDS activist?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he a leader?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because his professional duty was something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that the JNA in June or July 1991 captured the Batina bridge. And on the 25th or 26th of July, 1991, it captured Knezevi Vinogradi, or took control of it. Is there any dispute that in the period you're referring to, the SFRY was still in existence at the time the president of the Presidency was even Stjepan Mesic? So what kind of capture are you talking about? You mean that it controlled the bridge and the area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could accept such a change of the wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the JNA came to the areas where there were conflicts between Serbs and Croats, precisely those areas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you clarify that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it came to the areas where there were clashes between Serbs and Croats, in order to separate the two sides and to prevent conflicts between them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Baranja, there was only one such example, though in Baranja, there were virtually no conflicts during the takeover. The only conflict was in Beli Manastir between MUP units and armed Serbs which was stopped through the activity of armoured vehicles which didn't open fire but were set in motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So the army started the vehicles in order to preempt a conflict between the MUP of Croatia and the Serb territorials. It didn't even open fire, but as soon as the vehicles appeared, things calmed down and there were no conflicts. There were no other conflicts, were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm glad we've cleared that up. So what that means is the JNA did not interfere in those conflicts but prevented them on both sides?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that on the 6th of September, 1991, the inhabitants of Baranja formed two brigades and one artillery division because they were dissatisfied with the failure of the JNA to engage? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the date, but what you said is right, is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you perhaps know - though this is not in Baranja itself, that's why I'm asking you whether you may know, perhaps - that a JNA unit was positioned in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, 1991, between the clashing parties, virtually saved the Croatian police and paramilitary groups from total defeat and much greater casualties that could have occurred, that in that case, too, it acted to appease the tension and to put a stop to mutual fighting.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it immediately stopped hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into closed session for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned that some Croatian families went missing from your immediate vicinity, I should like to ask you whether you know that in the course of 1990, Branimir Glovac, the Osijek Jupan, or "count," on behalf of the HDZ, distributed in the municipalities of Slavonia very powerful military explosive called Vitezit. And the Croatian press reported about this, among others. Do you know anything about the blowing up of Serb houses? Do you know that some people even changed their first and last names, and do you know how many houses were blown up? Do you know anything at all about those events?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have some knowledge linked to such events, ranging from the blowing up of Serb houses, business premises owned by Serbs, the political newspaper offices, et cetera. There were such events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know exactly where they occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Osijek. This was closer to me and I was more familiar with the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the expression that was in use by -- I don't know how else to call them but terrorists or extremists in Eastern Slavonia, and members of these Ustasha formations which openly call themselves Ustashas and carried the letter "U" on them? Had you ever heard of them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You had heard about them. And do you know the expression they used from that time and from that area, that the Serbs had floated down to Serbia. Does that mean along the Danube?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our case, along the Drava.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of how many cases had you heard?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of some more prestigious Osijek doctors, physicians. Maybe I heard of seven or eight such cases, of more prestigious Serbs in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So Serbs who were prestigious, who were not members of any kind of militant structure or who could not be accused of any kind of militant attitude were killed and thrown into the Drava?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that only from the Beli Manastir municipality alone, 57 persons were killed and went missing in the period 1991 to 1993? I'm talking only about Serbs now.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the municipality of Beli Manastir or Beli Manastir itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Municipality of Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is also data of Veritas. I suppose you had occasion to see them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that members of the Zengas, across the Hungarian border, with the permission of the Hungarian authorities, crossed into Baranja on two occasions, the first time on the 30th of September, 1991, and the second time the 30th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an area that we've already mentioned, around the village of Torjanci which it was very difficult to control because of the swamp land there. And the Croatian army, across Hungarian territory, crossed over with the aim of taking control of the frontier posts in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that each and every one of them were captured precisely by the Territorial Defence and then handed over via the JNA to the Croatian side again? In other words, they were released, to return to their homes unscathed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. They entered a mine field, and they surrendered so as to avoid getting killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But nobody got killed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 30th of November, 1991, in the village of Torjanci in Baranja, members of that same army, the National Guards Corps, slaughtered a number of gypsies?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about that event? This was also in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they entered, and these were mostly locals who had left the village. They came back and spent the night in their own village. And during the night, they killed some people among whom most were non-Serbs. And again, there was an attempt to capture the border post and to stop a lorry transporting bread to that border post and to use that truck for that purpose, but they didn't succeed, though there were casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the Croatian forces killed 25 persons in the village of Torjanci. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the number, but there were victims. I think that the number 25 occurred in another operation on the 3rd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm talking about. This is a second operation. When they slit the throat of these gypsies, this was a previous operation in the same region. And then on the 3rd of April, 1992, they again attacked the same area and killed 25 persons.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this time also they came through the territory of Hungary. They used some anti-armour vehicles and came behind the back of the separation lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of their killing Zeljko Negovanovic on the 21st of August in the factory of cattle feed? He was working, he wasn't armed, he was an ordinary worker there, and he was killed because he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that particular detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in the police station yard in Darda, they killed Milivoj Stojakovic on Saint Elias Day, on the 2nd of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in that period, an assassination attempt was made at Ilija Djurkovic from Beli Manastir, who succumbed to his wounds on the 5th of September, and Nedo Tomic was seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedo, a man. Yes, I do know about that. I'm aware of that incident. And it provoked the Serbs to organise themselves in Karanac, in Knezevi Vinogradi immediately after that incident, and the villages were closed with checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 7th of September, 1991, a sabotage group of the National Guards mined the region around the Serb village of Balma. It's a Serb village. And four members of the defence of Baranja were killed, four TO members.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 14th of September, a sabotage group Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. came to the Jelen agricultural estate and killed two unarmed workers on the estate who were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can have five minutes more, until 10 past, and then you will have had much longer than the Prosecution, and we shall bring your cross-examination to a close.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. It is very difficult for me to ask all the questions I would like to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But without enumerating, many of these events you know about. People died from the constant onslaughts by the black-shirt groups of men, the extremists. All those events are events you know about. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So throughout that time, while you were working, did the Serbs ever attack any Croatian settlements or conduct crimes of this kind against a village, against the inhabitants of a village, against workers, citizens, or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In that period of time, the Serbs were exclusively oriented towards Defence, towards defending the lines taken, towards defending Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Then I need not question you any further on that score. I should just like to clarify one point, as our time is up and I have many more questions to ask, but the collective answer to all the questions, let's clear up one point, and that is concerning the document that I looked for a moment ago and wasn't able to find amongst all my documents. It is the document which speaks about the alleged abuse of a position on the side of the anti-terrorist ATD and the SUP in Baranja. This document is, in fact, titled "Explanation" and then it goes on to say "Abuse of position by members of the ATD, anti-terrorist operations, and the SUP, Secretariat of the Interior, in Baranja," and there is no signature to the document. So I don't know what value this document has at all. And does it mean anything to you as a witness?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document, as such, as a document, is one I saw for the first time here. However, the events that are described in the document mean something to me. I think that this is only a portion of the events that have been described in this document, not everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, as we noted a moment ago that the situation there was calm and that the Serbs were just defending themselves, protecting themselves, that there were no other - how shall I put this? - no other incidents, so what has it got to do with the Serb authorities at all, or with any conduct on the part of the organs and institutions of Baranja, Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem, the fact that somebody was stealing vehicles, for example, and selling those vehicles elsewhere or engaging in any other activities of that kind? What has that to do with any of the authorities in this trial and anything to do with this trial here? In view of the job you had, I'm sure you know how much the police of Serbia did to prevent all this happening, to prevent theft, looting, that it confiscated vehicles if perpetrators were engaged in unlawful import of such vehicles, that they had set up checkpoints and so on. Now, what has that got to do with our proceedings here and what we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must bring this to an end. We will allow the witness to answer. It's not for him to answer what it has to do with the proceedings, that's for us to decide because that's a question of relevance. But you can deal with two questions: Do you know any connection between this sort of activity, Witness C-025, under various authorities there may have been, apart from Colonel Mijovic, of course? You can answer that, if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was an interconnection in view of the fact that the units of Colonel Mijovic was not linked along the chain of command to the territory in which it was active, however Colonel Mijovic did have an influence on the leadership of the then SUP in Beli Manastir. Rather, they were the ones who carried out his orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other thing that was put is that efforts were made to stop this kind of activity going on. Can you help on that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were. But all this went on in bouts, in different periods. And it depended on what was going on in the realm of politics. For example, there were some periods in which this form of activity, when registration -- the re-registration of vehicles was allowed, and there were periods when it was not allowed, this attempt to register the vehicles without registration plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the authorities in Serbia ever allowed this take place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Serbia. I'm talking about Baranja, the Baranja territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We've clarified that. One more question now: In your statement on page 10, and you also spoke about this during the examination-in-chief, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, go into private session. This is the last question.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, list of witnesses next, please. There is a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last witness list is I think still valid, save for the fact it was made clear last week that Mr. Blewitt, even without his medical problem, would be used as a -- is to come after witnesses coming from outside --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could just remind us the order we've got them coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it would be Witness Laber next, followed by C -- yes, Poljanic is next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Laber, Poljanic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we get to it, I think it will be K-2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: K-2. And Mr. Blewitt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably now not this week I should think because we've only got until Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, with respect to the cross-examination conducted by Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, in case Mr. Nice in the event that Mr. Nice has no questions, then I will refrain from asking my questions and not keep the witness any longer, on condition that Mr. Nice has nothing further to ask the witness either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, have you got any questions? I mean, we have to keep the witness -- I'm afraid we have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have questions. I'm not sure about the propriety about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's totally improper. But nonetheless, have you got any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You do. So that's the answer. You must come back, I'm afraid, tomorrow morning but it won't be for very long, Witness C-025. 9.00 tomorrow morning, please.
